Add a key-schema version to the key name (or a migration/fallback) so old SET-typed keys cannot be touched as sorted sets.

The new ZADD writes sorted sets into the same span-buf:s namespace previously populated by SADD, without migrating existing set keys. During deployment, inserting into an existing buffered segment fails with WRONGTYPE, and the new ZSCAN reader likewise fails on pending old-format segments instead of flushing them. Introduce a coordinated migration/drain or a versioned namespace with compatible handling of pending old-format buffers.

issues.descricao: Claims zpopmin eviction can drop the root span while the has-root flag stays set, flushing a segment without its root.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: zpopmin eviction by lowest end_timestamp has no protection for the segment/root span. WHY: Root with smallest or tied timestamp (tests use identical timestamps, ties break lexicographically) is evicted while hrs flag stays 1, flushing a root-marked segment missing its root.

issues.descricao: max_segment_spans is still a constructor parameter but is no longer enforced; the segment cap is now hardcoded to 1000 in the Lua script, so the configured value is ignored.

comentarios.texto: This hunk removes the only load-time span-count cap (`self.max_segment_spans`): previously a segment exceeding 1001 spans was logged, deleted from `payloads`/`cursors`, and skipped, but now every scanned span is unconditionally appended via `payloads[key].extend(...)`. The new bound relies entirely on insert-time eviction in the Lua script; if that eviction fails to bound a key (e.g. duplicated/scored members or the concurrent-writer case the code itself warns about at lines 457-461), this method will now materialize an unbounded number of spans into memory and emit them, whereas before it was safely skipped. Re-introduce a span-count guard (or verify the invite-time eviction strictly caps cardinality) to keep memory bounded.

buffer.py declares the segment span limit as the configurable `max_segment_spans` (default 1001, line 150) and this hunk removed the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` size guard from the flush path, while the other changed file (add-buffer.lua line 62) now enforces a hardcoded cap of 1000 spans. The two changed files disagree on what the segment span limit is: the Lua cap (1000) is not the declared `max_segment_spans`, and the buffer no longer applies the declared limit at all. If `max_segment_spans` is configured below 1000 (or below the Lua cap), oversized segments that this code used to skip will now be flushed. Reconcile the constant: either keep/restore the buffer-side guard against `self.max_segment_spans`, or make the Lua cap derive from the same limit instead of hardcoding 1000.

The segment size cap is hardcoded as 1000 here, but SpansBuffer still declares max_segment_spans = 1001 in src/sentry/spans/buffer.py, and this PR deleted the flush-time guard that used that constant. The declared limit and the actually-enforced limit now disagree (and the Python constant is no longer honored anywhere). Make the Lua cap and the Python constant agree — either pass max_segment_spans in as an ARGV instead of the literal 1000, or update the declared constant to 1000 — so the buffer's enforced bound matches the value it declares.

issues.descricao: Tests give every span the same end timestamp and never exceed 1000 spans, so the new score ordering and oldest-first eviction are not tested.

comentarios.texto: All spans in the fixture use identical end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0, so the ZSET score-dependent behavior (ordering by end time, zunionstore score merge, and Lua zpopmin keeping newest 1000) is neutralised — tests pass even if scores are wrong or eviction keeps the wrong end. Use distinct timestamps and add a >1000-span trimming test asserting oldest evicted.
The missing test for the new trim path (zset ordering/trim by end_timestamp_precise, the >1000-span zpopmin path) is a coverage gap. Add a test that verifies the new trim behavior.

issues.descricao: Claims the redirect-resolution limit was silently cut from 10000 to 1000, so segment trees deeper than 1000 are no longer joined, and the comment still mentions 10k.

comentarios.texto: The loop bound was reduced from 10000 to 1000, but the comment on the line above still reads 'segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly'. The comment now contradicts the code it describes (the cap is 1000, i.e. depth ~1k); update it to match the new limit so readers are not misled about the redirect-walk depth.

The redirect-resolution loop limit was lowered from 10000 to 1000 with no explanation. For span trees deeper than 1000 the loop exits early, so set_span_id points to an intermediate node and the segment is split. Restore the previous limit, or make the new bound explicit and handled.
WHAT: Redirect-chase limit silently cut from 10000 to 1000. WHY: Segment trees with depth 1001-10000 previously joined correctly and now stop early, leaving split segments/redirects unresolved.

issues.descricao: Claims a non-root span whose key equals the resolved set key unions the key with itself and then unlinks it, deleting the buffered segment.

comentarios.texto: Handle `span_key == set_key` before merging/unlinking. Python now ZADDs the whole subsegment into the effective parent key before invoking this script. For a non-root span whose ID already resolves to that same set (for example a repeated span after its redirect was established), this branch unions the key with itself and then unlinks it, deleting the buffered segment. The sorted-set change additionally doubles its timestamp scores through the default SUM aggregation. Skip this merge/unlink when the keys are identical so the Python-produced buffer remains intact.

issues.descricao: Claims a span message missing end_timestamp_precise raises KeyError and aborts the whole batch.

comentarios.texto: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` indexes the field directly (unlike the adjacent `parent_span_id`, which uses `.get`). This consumer did not read `end_timestamp_precise` before this PR, so any ingest payload that omits the field (older/replayed producers, partial schema) previously processed fine but now raises KeyError and aborts the entire batch. Use `val.get("end_timestamp_precise")` with a fallback (e.g. a span timestamp or 0.0) or explicitly validate/skip payloads missing the field.

val["end_timestamp_precise"] is read with a hard key lookup. A span payload without this field raises KeyError in process_batch and fails the whole batch. Use val.get with a fallback (for example the batch timestamp), or skip the span.

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is a hard key lookup, so any span message that lacks the field raises KeyError in process_batch and fails the whole batch. The old code did not require this field. Read it with a fallback, for example `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", time.time())`, or skip the malformed span.

issues.descricao: Claims OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch passes cursor.offset directly into queryset slicing when advanced features are enabled.
issues.textoGolden: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.

issues.descricao: Claims BasePaginator.get_result sets start_offset to an unclamped offset for previous-page cursors, allowing negative slicing.
issues.textoGolden: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

issues.descricao: Claims OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies floor/ceil to a datetime key, raising TypeError.
issues.textoGolden: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.

issues.descricao: Claims accessing organization_context.member.has_global_access raises AttributeError when organization_context is None.
issues.textoGolden: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

sugestoes.texto: The match counter is updated with an unlocked read-modify-write. Two concurrent matches can read the same count and both save count + 1, causing the recorded number of blocked attempts to be too low. Update the counter atomically in SQL, or reload and update the record under a row lock.

The blocked-email lookup compares the submitted address exactly without normalizing its domain. UsersController#create passes params[:email] unchanged through User.new_from_params, so an address blocked as bad@example.com can sign up as bad@EXAMPLE.COM even though it delivers to the same mailbox. Normalize domain case consistently when storing blocked addresses and when looking them up.

The match counter is updated with an unlocked read-modify-write. If two signup validations match the same blocked email concurrently, both can load match_count = N, increment to N+1, and save, leaving N+1 despite two matches. This makes the persisted match statistics incorrect under concurrent requests. Increment the counter atomically in SQL (and update last_match_at in the same statement), or lock and reload the record before incrementing.

The lookup compares the email literally, while account flows use Email.downcase for email identity. For example, a blocked entry stored as `Block@SpamFromHome.org` will not match the corresponding normalized signup address. The new model accepts such entries without normalization, so case differences can make a blocked identity usable. Canonicalize both stored blocked addresses and lookup inputs using the same email normalization as User, and normalize existing entries (or perform a consistently case-insensitive lookup). Add a mixed-case regression test.

The regexp is not anchored to the end of the address. With a whitelist of `example.com`, `user@example.com.attacker.org` matches and is allowed even though its domain is not whitelisted. The same substring behavior can incorrectly reject unrelated domains when using the blacklist. Match the entire domain, not just its prefix.

issues.descricao: When the server rejects an email, the signup form marks it with the generic 'invalid email' text instead of the server's reason (blocked or not allowed).

comentarios.texto: The message shown for a rejected email disagrees with the reason the code is reacting to. This branch fires when the server rejected the email (result.errors.email), and this PR gives that condition its own server string — user.email.blocked, added in config/locales/server.en.yml as "is not allowed." — but the client re-labels it with the generic I18n.t('user.email.invalid'). A user whose address is perfectly well-formed but blocked/hosted on a blacklisted domain is therefore told their email is invalid, contradicting the reason just returned by the server. Use the blocked/not-allowed message (and add a matching client locale key) instead of user.email.invalid. Notice the same generic string is used at line ~94 for validation failures, so it should not be reused to represent a distinct server-side rejection.

issues.descricao: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks up the email with a case-sensitive exact match and no normalisation, so changing the letter case of a blocked address bypasses the block list.
issues.textoGolden: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

comentarios.texto: Blocked-email lookup compares the raw email without normalizing its domain. A signup for block@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG does not match a blocked record for block@spamfromhome.org despite identifying the same mailbox, allowing the signup restriction to be bypassed by changing domain capitalization. Normalize domains using Email.downcase both when storing blocked emails and when looking them up.

Canonicalize blocked emails consistently with the application's Email.downcase identity handling, both when storing entries and when looking them up. This exact equality query is case-sensitive, and BlockedEmail's validation callback only defaults action_type. A block-list entry such as `Block@SpamFromHome.org` therefore does not block the same identity submitted/stored as `block@spamfromhome.org`. This is particularly relevant to the explicitly supported manually populated block list. Normalize existing/imported entries as well as new ones, and add a test with differing casing between the stored entry and the lookup.
Case-sensitivity bypass: BlockedEmail.where(email: email) is exact case-sensitive with no normalization, while sibling checks are case-insensitive. Normalize (downcase/strip) on write and lookup.

issues.descricao: BlockedEmail.should_block? updates match_count and last_match_at as a side effect of email validation, so each signup attempt (validated twice) inflates the counter and concurrent updates can lose increments.
issues.textoGolden: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: should_block? mutates match_count/last_match_at via read-modify-write save inside a validator. WHY: Every validation call (including re-validations of the same attempt or attempts failing on unrelated fields like username) inflates stats, and concurrent signups lose increments with no atomic update. HOW: Move stats update out of validation or use atomic increment (update_counters/increment_counter) only on actual blocked rejections.

WHAT: `should_block?` mutates state (increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at`, calls `record.save`) inside a method that is invoked from the model validation callback, and the signup controller runs validation twice per attempt (`user.valid?` at users_controller.rb:168 then `user.save` at :172). WHY: a single signup attempt increments `match_count` twice and rewrites `last_match_at`, so the per-email block statistics the feature was built to track are wrong. HOW: make the read side non-mutating for validation and record the match separately (e.g. move the increment out of validation, or guard it so it runs once per attempt), keeping the predicate pure.

WHAT: `record.match_count += 1; record.last_match_at = ...; record.save` is a non-atomic read-modify-write with no lock or unique constraint protection. WHY: two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email can both read the same `match_count` and one write overwrites the other, losing counts, so the tracked statistics drift under load. HOW: use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ...')` or a database-level counter increment.

issues.descricao: Claims the 'returns false' spec cannot distinguish nil from false because be_false is a truthiness matcher.

comentarios.texto: This test is named "returns false if a record with the email doesn't exist," but it cannot verify that. `BlockedEmail.should_block?` returns `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]`, which yields `nil` (not `false`) when no record exists, and under this suite's RSpec 2 semantics `subject.should be_false` is a truthiness matcher that passes for any falsy value including `nil`. The assertion therefore passes on the nil the code actually returns and would only fail on an outright `true`; it does not pin the `false`/`nil` distinction its name asserts. Assert the value exactly (e.g. `subject.should == false`, or `be_falsey`/`be_nil` if nil is intended) so a regression returning a non-false falsy value is caught.

issues.descricao: The domain whitelist/blacklist regex @(domains) is not anchored at the end, so an address like user@example.com.evil.com matches a whitelist entry for example.com and bypasses the restriction.
issues.textoGolden: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: email_in_restriction_setting? builds unanchored Regexp "@(domains)" with only '.' escaped. WHY: Whitelist 'gmail.com' substring-matches 'victim@gmail.com.evil.com', so an attacker registers with an unapproved domain and bypasses the allow-list; blacklist similarly over/under-matches and other regex metachars are unescaped. HOW: Anchor and escape domains (e.g. Regexp.escape per domain split on '|' plus /\A[^@\s]+@(?:domain)\z/i).

issues.descricao: Claims the rejected-email memory stores the server-normalised email, so it never matches the raw input on retry.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Rejection memory pushes result.values.email (server-side user.attributes value) but checks contains(raw accountEmail). WHY: If server normalizes (strip/case) the email, normalized != raw input so contains() misses and the client-side invalid marker fails to trigger on retry. HOW: Push the attempted raw email (or normalize both sides before compare/push).

issues.descricao: Claims the 'rejectedEmails.@each' dependent key does not observe pushes of plain strings, so the rejection is not shown until the email changes.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: emailValidation depends on 'rejectedEmails.@each' while rejections are added via pushObject of plain strings. WHY: @each observes properties of array items, not membership, so pushing a string does not invalidate the computed property and the remembered rejection error does not display until accountEmail itself changes. HOW: Depend on 'rejectedEmails.[]' (or 'rejectedEmails.length').

Dependent key 'rejectedEmails.@each' will not invalidate when pushObject(result.values.email) adds a string; use 'rejectedEmails.[]' (or '.length'). As written the cached emailValidation won't recompute after a server email rejection, so the rejected email won't show inline invalid.

issues.descricao: BlockedEmail.should_block? returns nil instead of false when the email has no record.

comentarios.texto: `should_block?` is declared/used as a boolean predicate (its name, its use in the validator's boolean context, and `spec/models/blocked_email_spec.rb:23`'s `be_false`), but the expression `record && record.action_type == actions[:block]` returns `nil` when no record matches instead of `false`. Coerce the result to a real boolean (e.g. `record.present? && record.action_type == actions[:block]`), otherwise the method's return contract as declared by its consumer/spec is violated.

issues.descricao: Claims EmailValidator dropped the email format check that the old User#email_validator performed, allowing invalid emails.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: EmailValidator.validate_each performs no email syntax/format check, only whitelist/blacklist and blocked lookup. WHY: Any arbitrary string passes validation when no restriction is configured, regressing the moved User#email_validator contract and allowing invalid emails to create accounts. HOW: Restore format validation (e.g. regex / presence of @/domain) before restriction checks.

sugestoes.texto: Only the timeseries aggregation is upsampled; the top-events selection and ordering still use the original count(). Both discover.top_events_timeseries and errors.top_events_timeseries first select the limited groups using selected_columns and orderby, so a group with fewer stored events but a larger weighted count can be excluded from a chart that now displays weighted counts. Transform the count aggregation used for group selection and its corresponding ordering consistently with the timeseries aggregation.

The upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset, which is the dataset actually queried by this callback. get_event_stats_factory invokes this callback with discover for dashboard error-only queries even when the outer dataset is metrics-enhanced, so allowlisted error results on those paths remain unweighted. Pass scoped_dataset to the eligibility check and evaluate the effective query when deciding whether that Discover query is error-only.

The substring check treats negated and mixed-event queries as error-only queries. For example, !event.type:error and event.type:error OR event.type:transaction both enable the sample_weight aggregate on Discover even though they include non-error events, violating the helper's error-only contract and replacing their normal count aggregation. Determine eligibility from parsed query conditions and require that the full expression restricts results to error events.

The substring test also returns True for `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`. Neither query is restricted to errors, but for allowlisted projects this replaces count() with the error-specific sample-weight aggregation. This violates the stated error-only guard and can give incorrect counts for mixed/non-error results. Determine whether the parsed filter actually restricts results to errors, rather than looking for the token anywhere in the raw query.

issues.descricao: The upsampling decision is evaluated against the request's dataset instead of the scoped_dataset actually queried, so in the dashboard discover-split path (metrics dataset) error queries run against discover skip upsampling even when all projects are allowlisted.
issues.textoGolden: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

comentarios.texto: The upsampling decision uses the closure variable `dataset` while the transformed `final_columns` are executed against `scoped_dataset`. In the dashboard-split path `_get_event_stats` is deliberately invoked with a different dataset (e.g. `_get_event_stats(discover, ...)` at lines 351, 365, 406, 423) than the request's `dataset`, so the `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` branch can be evaluated against the wrong dataset and apply/skip `sum(sample_weight)` for a dataset that was never queried. Base the decision on the dataset actually being queried (`scoped_dataset`) so the transform matches the target of the query.

issues.descricao: _is_error_focused_query uses a substring match for `event.type:error` on the request query, so negated or mixed (OR transaction) discover queries are treated as error-only and get the sample_weight sum instead of count().

comentarios.texto: `_is_error_focused_query` decides whether to apply `upsampled_count()` by doing a naive substring search for `event.type:error` in the raw request query. A query that excludes errors (e.g. `!event.type:error`) or the discover-split query `({query}) AND event.type:transaction` still contains the literal `event.type:error`, so the transform is applied to a non-error / transactions query, summing `sample_weight` where it should be a plain `count()` and producing wrong bucket values. It also ignores the actual `query` passed to `_get_event_stats`, so the decision can differ from the query that is really executed. Match on a parsed/negation-aware condition (or pass the resolved query string) instead of a raw substring test.

The substring check treats `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` as error-only queries. For allowlisted projects this rewrites count() to an aggregation over sample_weight even when the Discover query includes transactions, violating the error-only restriction and potentially failing against a transaction-backed query. Determine the event-type restriction from the parsed query rather than the presence of a substring.

Substring matching does not establish that the Discover query selects only errors. For example, `!event.type:error` and `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` both return True here, causing count() to be replaced with the sample-weight aggregation for non-error or mixed results in allowlisted projects. This contradicts the error-only guard and can produce incorrect counts. Parse the query and establish an error-only restriction (including negation and Boolean structure), or conservatively skip transformation when that restriction cannot be proven.

issues.descricao: test_error_upsampling_with_transaction_events cannot detect upsampling being applied to transaction queries, because the transaction has no sample_weight and upsampled_count() equals count() for it.

The transaction event has no sample_weight, and upsampled_count uses ifNull(sample_weight, 1), so the result is still 1 and 0. issues.descricao: GetWebAssets does not re-check the cache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent callers that missed the cache each reload the assets manifest.
issues.textoGolden: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: The exclusive lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer on line 49) across the blocking file read / synchronous CDN HTTP request (lines 56-67) and there is no re-check of entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock. WHY: On a cold cache, all concurrent callers (api/index.go:82, api/frontendsettings.go:62, middleware/recovery.go:141) block on the write lock and then each sequentially re-executes the full load (file I/O or blocking http.DefaultClient.Do), producing a thundering-herd serialization and N redundant loads instead of one; in Dev mode this happens on every request since the fast path is skipped, serializing all concurrent page loads. HOW: after `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` re-check the cache (`if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }`) so only the first goroutine performs the load, and drop the defer in favor of releasing the lock immediately after assigning `entryPointAssetsCache = result` to avoid holding it during I/O.
cache is not re-checked under the lock after re-acquiring write Lock, so concurrent callers can each recompute web assets

The cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent production requests that initially observe a nil cache each reload and decode the manifest even after another request has populated it. During a cold-start request burst, these redundant filesystem reads and JSON decodes execute serially under the global lock, delaying queued page and frontend-settings requests and blocking cache readers while each reload runs. After acquiring the write lock, return the populated cache when cfg.Env != setting.Dev before performing asset loading.

issues.textoGolden: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

comentarios.texto: The cache is assigned unconditionally, so when readWebAssetsFromFile fails, a nil result overwrites a previously valid cached value, and every caller then gets (nil, err). Only assign entryPointAssetsCache when err == nil and result != nil. On error, return the error and leave the existing cache untouched.

issues.descricao: Claims holding the exclusive lock across file and CDN I/O serializes all GetWebAssets callers.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: Exclusive entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() is held across blocking file read (readWebAssetsFromFile) and HTTP fetch (readWebAssetsFromCDN). WHY: Serializes all concurrent GetWebAssets callers on disk/network latency and blocks RLock fast-path readers behind the pending writer; in Dev mode where the cache is bypassed every request serializes on file I/O. HOW: Load outside the exclusive lock (double-check, load, then lock only to publish) or use singleflight/sync.Once for the cold-miss path.

issues.descricao: get_failure_reason's docstring examples do not match the strings the function returns.

The singular branch (line 146) returns a `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` value such as "A missed check-in was detected", yet the docstring advertises "A failed check-in was detected"; the multi-check-in branch joins `"%(count)d %(status)s"` fragments with `get_text_list(..., last_word=_("and"))` and appends " check-ins detected", yielding "2 missed and 1 error check-ins detected", not the docstring's "2 missed check-ins, 1 timeout check-in and 1 error check-in were detected". Update the examples (or the format string) so the documented contract matches the code.

issues.descricao: get_monitor_environment_context builds a config copy with the human-readable schedule_type but returns the original monitor.config, so the conversion is lost and the context shows the raw value.
issues.textoGolden: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config to `config` and converts schedule_type display, but returns the original monitor_environment.monitor.config instead of `config`. WHY: the display conversion never takes effect so the occurrence context carries the raw schedule_type value, producing wrong output vs the function's evident intent. HOW: return `"config": config` instead of `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config`.

Dead computation: `config` is copied and `config['schedule_type']` transformed to display value, but return uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (original) instead of `config`. Change to `"config": config` so transformation is used.

WHAT: In get_monitor_environment_context the code copies config and replaces config['schedule_type'] with the human-readable get_schedule_type_display(), but the returned context dict uses the original `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the modified local `config`, so the mutation is dead. WHY: The occurrence's monitor context always reports the raw schedule_type value rather than the display string the code intended to substitute, producing incorrect evidence data in the emitted occurrence. HOW: return the local variable, i.e. use "config": config in the returned dict.

issues.descricao: Claims previous_checkins[0] can raise IndexError when the threshold query returns no rows.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: starting_checkin = previous_checkins[0] indexes without an empty-list guard when the threshold>1 query returns no rows. WHY: raises IndexError and crashes the mark_failed/consumer path when the failed check-in is not visible to the date_added__lte filter (unsaved/synthetic check-in, clock skew, or race). HOW: guard with if not previous_checkins: return False before indexing.

issues.descricao: Asks to confirm no consumer still imports SimpleCheckIn from mark_failed after it moved to monitors/types.py.

comentarios.texto: `SimpleCheckIn` was moved out of `src/sentry/monitors/logic/mark_failed.py` into this module. Any consumer that still does `from sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed import SimpleCheckIn` (the old home of this symbol) will now fail with an ImportError at module load. The new in-tree consumers (`monitors/logic/incidents.py`, `monitors/logic/incident_occurrence.py`) were updated to import from `sentry.monitors.types`, but confirm there is no other importer left referencing the old location (e.g. tests or addon code); if there is, update it to import `SimpleCheckIn` from `sentry.monitors.types`.
